sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the headline "When new tickets arrive", then drops straight to the red and orange band in the middle of the weekday rows. From there it moves right to the big numbers. This reads as an internal report screen for a support team lead, and it feels calm and orderly. Assumed job: show a support manager when tickets arrive so they can plan staffing.

The whole piece:
- Can a viewer say in one sentence what it's for? yes
- Do the image and headline make one idea? yes
- Does every element do a job? yes
- Do type, colour and shape share one mood? yes
- Is the copy finished? **no**. "Busiest hour, weekdays 10:00" disagrees with the chart, where the only red cells sit in the 11:00 column. "New tickets, September 3,412" also covers a different date range from the chart's "1 to 28 September".
- Does each kind of element look the same everywhere? yes
- Do the colours carry the right mood? yes. The rainbow scale itself is left to the colour and data sections.
- Does each heading name what its section holds? yes

The one `no` line has no catalog entry, so there are no entries to open, and I judged it as common sense.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the copy finished, with no placeholder text and no spelling mistakes?** No. The side panel says "Busiest hour, weekdays / 10:00" (about x 1034–1180, y 315–375), but the chart points to 11:00.
   - **Where:** The time labels line up with the columns. "09:00" sits over column 9 (x ≈ 430–466). The only two red "30+" cells (Mon and Fri) are in the 11:00 column (x ≈ 506–542), and the 10:00 column is orange "25–29" on every weekday. In the cropped view, 11:00 is red or orange on every weekday, so it is at least as busy as 10:00.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** they see the red peak, read "10:00" beside it, and conclude that either the stat or the chart is wrong. In a report used for staffing, that doubt spreads to every number on the page.
   - **Is it really wrong?** Not necessarily. The colour bins can hide the true numbers: 10:00 could average 29 a day while 11:00 has a few 30s and 25s. But nothing on the page tells the viewer that.
   - **Fix:** check the figure. If 11:00 is the real peak, correct the stat. If 10:00 is right, say how it was worked out ("highest weekday average, 29/hr") so the stat explains the chart instead of contradicting it.
   - **Smaller copy issue:** the stat "New tickets, September 3,412" sits next to a chart subtitle that says "1 to 28 September". The viewer can't tell whether 3,412 covers the same 28 days or the whole month. Make the ranges match, or name the range in the stat.
   - **Filing:** if the director files chart-versus-label agreement under Charts and data, this belongs there.
   - Defect (common sense, no catalog entry). Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The headline and the chart are one idea. "When new tickets arrive" asks the exact question the heatmap answers, and the subtitle sets the measure, scope and time span in one line. A first-time viewer knows what they are looking at within seconds.
- The page holds together. One sans-serif typeface, one restrained grey layout and one repeated stat-block pattern (label, big number, comparison) keep the side panel and chart reading as one report rather than a collage.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (copy finished: the "busiest hour" stat contradicts the chart, and the September total covers a different range from the chart).

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The three KPI figures in the right column ("3,412" at about x 1034–1105, y 232–258; "10:00" at y≈328–354; "42 min" at y≈424–450) look about 26 px bold. The page title "When new tickets arrive" (x 40–370, y≈97–125) looks about 28 px bold. These are two different jobs: the title says what the page is, and the KPIs are side figures. But they share almost the same size, weight and dark color. After the heatmap, the eye has no clear second stop and moves between the title and the KPI column. The right column reads as if it were as important as the page heading, and the title loses some of its authority. Under Müller-Brockmann's and Lupton's "Visual hierarchy has distinct levels", each level should be told from the next at a glance, and sizes only a few pixels apart read as an accident (Bringhurst on scales). There are two ways to fix it:
   - Make the title clearly the top level by opening a real step above the KPIs (title around 32–36 px, KPIs as they are).
   - Or step the KPI figures down (around 20–22 px), so they sit as a secondary level under the title. The labels and the "Up 4% on August" lines already separate them well.

   This is a convention breach with a small cost, so it is minor. The page still works, and the heatmap carries the main focus.

**What's working.**
- **The chart is the focal point, as it should be.** The warm red and orange band (about x 430–750, y 212–400) is the strongest contrast on the page. The answer to the title's question ("when do tickets arrive?") is the first thing the eye lands on.
- **The small text is ranked by color and weight, not by more sizes.** The KPI labels, the "Same as August" lines, the axis labels, the legend values and the source line all sit at one small size (about 12–13 px) in muted gray. The bold "New tickets per hour" legend label and the bold KPI figures give emphasis through weight. This keeps the scale short and avoids a pile of near-equal sizes.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (distinct text levels: the KPI figures are almost the same size and weight as the page title).

Sizes are estimated by eye from the image; I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts because Bash was denied in this session. I read the reference entry directly instead.

**Walk (working notes)**

The image is about 1280×800 px, one screen, so I worked from the whole image. I couldn't run the crop script because Bash is denied.

First read: the eye lands on the red and orange band at 10:00–11:00 on weekdays (x≈468–582, y≈212–400). It then goes up to the headline "When new tickets arrive" and finally to the three numbers on the right. This reads as a reporting screen for support leads, used to plan staffing. It feels calm and orderly.

Arrangement and space:
- One grid: yes. The title, subtitle, source and row labels share x=40. The heatmap, hour labels and legend title share x=88. The first legend swatch starts at x=278, which is a heatmap column edge. The stats column has its own edge at x=1034.
- No near-misses: yes. The top of the first stat label (y≈213) lines up with the top of the heatmap (y=212). The other stat blocks are clearly off the row lines, not almost on them. Hour labels sit on their column edges.
- Baselines across columns: yes. No running text sits side by side.
- Space inside groups smaller than between groups: yes. Title and subtitle are about 25 px apart, and the chart is about 45 px below them. Each stat's label, number and delta are tight, with about 45 px between stats.
- Boxes hold one group: yes. There are no boxes, only the rule under the nav.
- No accidental groups: yes.
- No overlaps: yes.
- Margin from edge: yes, 40 px.
- Space gathered: yes. It sits in one band under the content and one area under the stats column.
- Balance: yes.
- Centering by habit: yes, none.
- Proportion: yes. A wide chart with a narrow side column is a standard main-plus-sidebar split.
- Eye path: yes. The hot spot leads to the title, then the stats. Nothing leads off the edge.

No line was answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** 
- **Shared edges.** The page uses a few edges and sticks to them. Everything outside the chart (title, subtitle, row labels, source) sits on x=40, and the chart, its hour labels and the legend title sit on x=88. The legend's first swatch starts at x=278, which is itself a heatmap column edge. Because of this, the legend reads as part of the chart rather than a separate widget. Keep these shared edges if the layout changes.
- **The stats column's spacing.** The first stat's label sits level with the top of the heatmap (y≈212). Each stat's label, number and delta are tightly packed, with clearly bigger gaps (about 45 px) between stats. The three numbers read as three separate facts that belong to the chart, with no box around them.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the 24-column heatmap and the side column reflow at narrower widths. The stats will probably drop below the chart, or the cells will shrink until they're too small to read.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes): Text**

Image is about 1280×800, roughly one screen. Bash is refused, so I'm working from the whole image only.

First read: the eye lands on the rainbow heatmap, then the title, then the three KPI numbers on the right. It reads as an internal support-analytics report page.

1. Body text large enough: yes. The subtitle is about 16 px, and the nav is the same size.
2. Captions and labels large enough: yes. Day, hour and legend labels look about 12 px and the source line about 13 px, which is small but readable on the web.
3. Plain reading face: yes. It is a single grotesque throughout.
4. One type plan: yes. One family is used in two weights.
5. Small text weight: yes. It is regular weight, not hairline.
6. Contrast: yes. The grey labels and the KPI sublines look dark enough. No pale text is visible.
7. Text over image: yes. There is none.
8. Line length: yes. The only long line is the one-line source note of about 140 characters, which is a caption, not a paragraph.
9. Leading: yes. There are no multi-line paragraphs.
10. Multi-line heading: yes. There is none.

13. Rag: yes. There is none.
14. Widows: yes.
15. Heading breaks: yes.
16. Paragraph marks: yes.
17. Left edge crisp: yes. The title, subtitle, nav brand and source line share x≈40.
18. Long text chunked: yes. There is no long text.
19. Mixed case: yes.
20. Emphasis: yes. "Reports" in the nav is bold only, and "New tickets per hour" is bold only.
21. Display spacing: yes. The title looks set slightly tight.
22. Kerning: yes.
23. Tracking: yes.
24. Caps letterspaced: yes. There are no strings of capitals.

26. Real cuts: yes. The bold looks like the true cut.

30. Nothing clipped: yes.

No line answered `no` or `unsure`, so I did not need to open any reference entries.

Outside the checklist, I checked the copy against the chart. "Busiest hour, weekdays: 10:00" disagrees with the grid: the red 30+ cells for Mon and Fri sit in the column after 10:00, which is 11:00. "New tickets, September" doesn't match the subtitle's "1 to 28 September".

---

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**

The checklist found nothing. Every Text line is yes. Two copy problems fall outside the checklist; the director may want to merge them with the Data section.

1. **The KPI copy contradicts the chart (not a checklist line).**
   - **Where:** "Busiest hour, weekdays / 10:00" (x≈1034–1180, y≈308–372).
   - **The mismatch:** the hour labels sit at the left edge of each cell (00:00 at x≈90 over the first cell, 09:00 at x≈432 over the tenth). That puts the only red 30+ cells, Mon and Fri at x≈506–542, in the 11:00 column. The 10:00 column is orange (25–29).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** anyone who checks the headline number against the chart finds they disagree. They then stop trusting one or the other, and staffing decisions depend on this number.
   - **Possible causes:** either the label means "10:00–11:00" and the axis labels are offset, or the copy is wrong.
   - **Fix:** make the KPI and the axis say the same hour. If the KPI averages across weekdays, say so explicitly ("10:00–11:00, Mon–Fri average").
   - **Type and weight:** defect, major.
2. **The copy names two different periods (not a checklist line).**
   - **Where:** the subtitle says "average week, 1 to 28 September" (y≈148), but the KPI says "New tickets, September" with "3,412" (y≈219–245).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** they can't tell whether 3,412 covers the same 28 days as the chart or the whole month, so they can't connect the total to the grid.
   - **Fix:** use one stated period for both, e.g. "New tickets, 1–28 September".
   - **Type and weight:** defect, minor.

**What's working.**
- **One family, few levels.** A single face carries a clear scale: a bold title of about 28 px, about 16 px for the subtitle and nav, a bold KPI figure of about 26 px, and about 12–13 px for labels and the source. Hierarchy comes from size and weight rather than from extra faces.
- **A source line that answers the questions you'd ask.** It says which clock the times are in and that hours mean when a ticket was opened, not when it was answered. That's exactly the misreading this chart invites, and the note heads it off.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The apostrophe in "team's" in the source line is too small to tell curly from straight without a crop (cropping was unavailable). This is minor; check it in the live page.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies. Outside the chart, the page uses only neutrals: near-black and gray type on white, with a hairline under the nav. Almost all the colour on the page is the heatmap's seven-step scale. That scale is chart colour, so the checklist files any problem with it under "Charts and data", not here. The data critic should look at it: it runs blue, teal, green, yellow, orange, red, and its lightness does not rise in step with the value, so yellow (20–24) is the lightest step and the blue for 0–4 sits almost as dark as the red. In grayscale the busiest hours would not read as the darkest or the strongest.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The page around the chart has no colour of its own: no accent on the nav, the "Reports" tab or the three numbers on the right. That makes the heatmap the only colour on the screen, so the eye goes straight to it, and the 3,412 / 10:00 / 42 min column holds its place through size and weight instead of competing in colour. Keep the page neutral even if the chart's scale changes.
- The heatmap cells are separated by thin white gaps, so strong neighbours like red and orange (Mon and Fri, around 11:00) or yellow and green never touch. Their edges stay clean with no vibration, even at full saturation.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

The only thing close to a mark is "Northlight Desk" at the top left (about x 40–178, y 18–38), and it's set as bold text in the nav, not as a drawn logo. The heatmap is a chart, so it belongs under the data section, not this one.

None.

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies. There is one day × hour heatmap and three headline figures.

**Findings**
1. **Does each chart's palette fit its data, an ordered lightness ramp for ordered values, a neutral midpoint for diverging values, and distinct hues for categories?** The grid (x≈88–998, y≈212–476) and the legend (x≈278–708, y≈504–518) use seven rainbow colours (periwinkle, cyan, teal, green, yellow, orange, red) for one count that runs from low to high. The colours do not get steadily darker as the count rises. Yellow (20–24) is the lightest and brightest step, so the 09:00 and 12:00–15:00 cells pop out about as much as the red 30+ cells. Meanwhile the quietest bin (0–4) is a heavy, saturated periwinkle that fills about 70% of the grid. Most of the colour on the page goes to the hours when nothing happens. A viewer can't see "more" at a glance and has to check each colour against the legend to rank cells. Wilke (*Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, ch. 19.2 and 4.2) calls for a sequential palette for ordered values. Approved fix: use one hue that goes from light to dark, so the colour order follows the value order (Wilke). Here that means near-white or pale for 0–4 and darkest for 30+, so the quiet night hours drop back and the busy weekday morning stands out by itself. Convention, and a defect in effect, because it misleads the ranking. **Major.**

2. **Can each chart's series be told apart without color vision, by labels, shapes, or a color-blind-safe palette such as Okabe-Ito?** Three neighbouring steps are hard to tell apart for red-green colour-blind viewers: green 15–19, orange 25–29 and red 30+, plus yellow 20–24 next to green. These are exactly the steps that separate busy from peak (columns 09:00–16:00 on weekdays). The cells carry no numbers, so colour is the only way to read the value (WCAG 1.4.1). Direction: the light-to-dark ramp from finding 1 fixes most of this because it orders the steps by lightness. You could also print the count in the peak cells, or on hover if the page is interactive. Defect. **Major**, since it comes from the same palette as finding 1.

3. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** The title "When new tickets arrive" (x≈40, y≈111) and the subtitle name the topic only. The finding, roughly "Tickets peak 10:00–12:00 on weekdays; weekends and nights are quiet", is left for the viewer to work out from the colours. The "Busiest hour" figure partly says it, but off to the side. Direction: put the takeaway in the title or the subtitle, so a staffing reader gets the answer before decoding the grid. Taste (the catalog's source is not on the approved list; common sense for a report someone acts on). **Minor.**

4. **(Not a checklist line: the figure and the chart disagree.)** "Busiest hour, weekdays: 10:00" (x≈1034, y≈315–366) doesn't match the grid. Going by the tick labels (09:00 starts at x≈430, cells about 38 px wide), the only red 30+ cells are in the 11:00 column (x≈505–542) on Mon and Fri. That column is orange on Tue–Thu. The 10:00 column (x≈468–504) is orange on all five weekdays, so 11:00 has the higher weekday average. Either the figure is wrong, or the tick labels are off by one column, or "busiest hour" is worked out differently from the grid. Any of these makes a reader distrust both. Pixel positions are by eye; the crop tool could not be run. Direction: check the figure against the data. If it is right, label the ticks at cell centres (or label every hour) so each column is clearly tied to its hour. Defect. **Major**, because staffing would be planned around the wrong hour.

**What's working.**
- Days by hours is the right form for "when do tickets arrive". Weekday vs weekend and morning vs night show as a shape at once, and Mon–Sun with 00:00–23:00 keeps the natural order.
- All three headline figures carry a period and a comparison with August ("Up 4%", "Same as August", "Down 6 min"), so the reader can tell good from bad without looking anything up.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the cells show exact counts on hover or focus. If they do, finding 2 is less serious for mouse users.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 14 yes, 2 no (palette fits the data, readable without colour vision), 0 unsure. On re-tally the walk has three `no` lines: palette, colour vision, and title states finding. Corrected: Charts and data: 16 lines, 13 yes, 3 no (palette fits the data; readable without colour vision; title states the finding), 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the four top-nav links. There are no buttons, fields or filters.

**Findings**
1. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** No. The heatmap and the three stats are locked to the scope in the subtitle (y≈148): "all queues, average week, 1 to 28 September". There is no period picker, queue filter, or export anywhere on the page. A support lead who reads this to plan staffing will want to ask "is this the same for my Billing queue?" or "how did August look?" next. Today they have no way to ask either from here. The right column even compares against August in words ("Up 4% on August", "Same as August", "Down 6 min on August") but gives no way to see August. Nielsen's heuristic 7 (*10 Usability Heuristics*) says frequent actions should have accelerators such as filters. Fix: add a compact control row between the subtitle and the grid, around y≈170, with a date-range or month picker and a queue selector. Keep it light so the heatmap stays the focus, and keep the subtitle in sync with whatever is selected. Convention. Weight: major. Without it the page answers one fixed question and can't be used for the follow-up questions a staffing decision needs. If this is a static emailed report and not a live screen, it's fine as it is. The top nav says it's a live app, though.

**What's working.**
- The current place is marked. "Reports" (x≈366–423, y≈27) is set bolder and darker than Queues, Agents and Settings. That's the single clear cue NN/g's menu-design checklist asks for, and the H1 names what's on the page.
- The page puts the answer in front of the user. The right column (x≈1034, y≈215–470) pulls out the busiest hour and the reply time, each with a comparison, so the manager doesn't have to dig the answer out of 168 cells. The source line (y≈573) explains up front that hours are when a ticket was opened, not answered, which heads off the most likely misreading.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicator on the nav links (is it at least 2 px with 3:1 contrast?) and their hover state. Check both in a live browser.
- Whether the heatmap cells are interactive (tooltips with exact counts on hover). If they are, nothing on the page signals it. If they aren't, the user can only read values from the 7-step legend bins.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 1 no (shortcuts for frequent actions), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
